#!/bin/sh
set -eu

# The harness-run convention (ADR 0086 §3): the runtime types
# `discobox-harness-run [--resume] '<prompt>'` into the terminal's login shell.
#
# The prompt trails a resume too (ADR 0086 §4), so a user whose first launch
# failed can still see what the sandbox was asked to do. This session already
# contains it, so `--continue` replaces it rather than sending it a second time.
if [ "${1-}" = "--resume" ]; then
	set -- --continue
else
	# A prompt is one prompt, however many words the shell split it into: the
	# command is typed, so `discobox run . fix the failing tests` arrives here
	# as four arguments. Joining everything after the flags back together with
	# single spaces is the wrapper's half of the convention (ADR 0086 §3) —
	# `claude` takes its prompt as a single positional and would otherwise be
	# asked to "fix".
	if [ "$#" -gt 1 ]; then
		prompt="$1"
		shift
		for word in "$@"; do
			prompt="$prompt $word"
		done
		set -- "$prompt"
	fi
fi

# Claude Code's memory lives in the primary source's durable data, keyed by the
# uid the way the pool cache is (ADR 0094): every sandbox on a source mounts the
# same tree whatever uid it runs as, so sandboxes that agree on a uid share
# memories, and one that does not can neither write the other's files nor take
# them over. The mount's root is chowned to whoever created a sandbox last, so
# the partition is made through sudo rather than depending on who owns its
# parent.
#
# The path names the uid, so the image's static managed settings cannot carry
# it. The launcher writes it as a managed-settings drop-in instead: policy, like
# the rest of the image's Claude Code settings, so a `claude` typed into any
# shell afterwards finds the same memory, `.claude/settings.json` (which the
# configure flow replaces) never holds it, and nothing that file says outranks
# it.
SOURCE_DATA=/.discobox/data-per-source/primary
MANAGED_DROP_INS=/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d
USER_DATA="$SOURCE_DATA/users/$(id -u)"
MEMORIES="$USER_DATA/harnesses/claude-code/memories"
# Where memories lived before they were keyed by uid. They are carried over
# only to the uid that owns them, never claimed by another.
LEGACY_MEMORIES="$SOURCE_DATA/harnesses/claude-code/memories"

if [ -d "$SOURCE_DATA" ]; then
	if sudo -n install -d -m 0755 "$SOURCE_DATA/users" &&
		sudo -n install -d -o "$(id -u)" -g "$(id -g)" -m 0700 "$USER_DATA"; then
		if [ ! -e "$MEMORIES" ] && [ -d "$LEGACY_MEMORIES" ] &&
			[ "$(stat -c %u "$LEGACY_MEMORIES")" = "$(id -u)" ]; then
			mkdir -p "$(dirname "$MEMORIES")"
			cp -a "$LEGACY_MEMORIES" "$MEMORIES" ||
				printf '%s\n' "discobox: could not carry over Claude Code memories from $LEGACY_MEMORIES" >&2
		fi
		mkdir -p "$MEMORIES"

			! printf '{"autoMemoryDirectory":"%s"}\n' "$MEMORIES" |
			sudo -n tee "$MANAGED_DROP_INS/discobox-memory.json" >/dev/null; then
			printf '%s\n' "discobox: could not record source-scoped Claude Code memories; using local storage" >&2
		fi
	else
		printf '%s\n' "discobox: could not prepare source-scoped Claude Code memories; using local storage" >&2
	fi
fi

# image_version prints the version of the agent the image itself installed, or
# nothing if it cannot be found. Nothing is pinned in that case (cmd_pin): the
# store may only be preferred when it is demonstrably newer.
image_version() {
	# Deliberately word-split: the setting is a search path, not one directory.
	# shellcheck disable=SC2086
	set -- ${AGENT_IMAGE_DIRS:-/usr/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules}
	for image_dir in "$@"; do
		if [ -r "$image_dir/$AGENT_PACKAGE/package.json" ]; then
			# `q` after the first match rather than `| head -1`: this runs in
			# the login sequence, where a saved process is a saved fork. The
			# address demands the whole shape the substitution does — key,
			# colon, opening quote — so a line it selects is always a line the
			# substitution fires on, and `q` cannot quit on a nested "version"
			# key having printed nothing.
			sed -n '/^[[:space:]]*"version"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"/{s/^[[:space:]]*"version"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p;q;}' \
				"$image_dir/$AGENT_PACKAGE/package.json"
			return 0
		fi
	done
}

# is_version is the one answer to "is this directory a usable version", and
# every reader here asks it — store_versions, fetch and prune. They disagreed
# once: fetch tested `[ -d ]` while the others tested the executable, and a
# directory that existed without one wedged the store permanently. npm view kept
# naming that version, fetch kept seeing a directory and skipping, nothing could
# pin it and nothing rebuilt it.
is_version() {
	[ -x "$dir/$1/bin/$AGENT_BIN" ]
}

# store_versions prints one version directory name per line. A half-built or
# half-deleted tree is not a version: it is never listed, never pinned, and
# prune deletes it as wreckage.
store_versions() {
	[ -d "$dir" ] || return 0
	for entry in "$dir"/*; do
		version=${entry##*/}
		case $version in
		'*' | .*) continue ;;
		esac
		is_version "$version" || continue
		printf '%s\n' "$version"
	done
}

newest_version() {
	store_versions | sort -V | tail -1
}

# newer_than A B is true when A sorts above B. Version strings, so sort -V.
newer_than() {
	[ "$1" != "$2" ] || return 1
	[ "$(printf '%s\n%s\n' "$1" "$2" | sort -V | tail -1)" = "$1" ]
}

# worth_fetching is true only for a version this pool could actually end up
# running: one above both the store's newest and the image's own copy.
#
# `npm view <pkg> version` answers the `latest` dist-tag, and a tag is a pointer,
# not a high-water mark — a vendor who ships a bad release moves it *back*.
# Without this, that costs a fetch of 100+ MiB, which prune then deletes on the
# next line of the same function, because a version that just landed has no pin
# and does not sort into the newest two. Every window. Forever, until the vendor
# publishes above the store again, and silently, because the refresh is
# detached. The same test skips a fetch the image already satisfies: §2 pins the
# store only when it beats the image, so a version below it would be downloaded
# for nobody.
#
# The alternative — keeping the tagged version whatever it sorts as — would have
# redefined retention and still not have been pinned, since §2 pins the newest
# in the store rather than the tagged one. Declining to fetch makes a rollback a
# no-op instead, which is what "a pin is for life and the newest wins" already
# implies.
worth_fetching() {
	reference=$(newest_version)
	image=$(image_version)
	if [ -n "$image" ] && { [ -z "$reference" ] || newer_than "$image" "$reference"; }; then
		reference=$image
	fi
	[ -n "$reference" ] || return 0
	newer_than "$1" "$reference"
}

# sandbox_id names this sandbox in a version's pins/ directory. The manifest is
# the authority; a sandbox running outside one (a bare `docker run` debug
# session) falls back to its hostname, which is only ever used to decide whether
# a version is still in use.
sandbox_id() {
	id=$(sed -n '/"sandboxId"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"/{s/.*"sandboxId"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p;q;}' \
		/etc/discobox/sandbox.json 2>/dev/null) || id=
	if [ -z "$id" ]; then
		id=$(hostname 2>/dev/null) || id=unknown
	fi
	printf '%s' "$id"
}

# touch_pin records that this sandbox is using a version. Retention reads the
# mtime, so this runs on every login rather than only when the pin is created:
# it is the only way one sandbox can tell another is still on a version.
touch_pin() {
	[ -d "$dir/$1" ] || return 0
	mkdir -p "$dir/$1/pins" 2>/dev/null || return 0
	touch "$dir/$1/pins/$(sandbox_id)" 2>/dev/null || true
}

# pinned_version prints the store version this sandbox is pinned to, or nothing
# if the link is absent or points somewhere else — a link the sandbox's own user
# put there is somebody's deliberate choice, and is not ours to read or replace.
pinned_version() {
	[ -L "$link" ] || return 0
	target=$(readlink "$link")
	case $target in
	"$dir"/*) ;;
	*) return 0 ;;
	esac
	target=${target#"$dir"/}
	printf '%s' "${target%%/*}"
}

cmd_pin() {
	pinned=$(pinned_version)
	if [ -n "$pinned" ]; then
		# Already pinned. Keep the version this sandbox is running, whatever
		# the store has moved on to, and just say it is still in use.
		touch_pin "$pinned"
		return 0
	fi
	# A link into the store under another package's directory is a pin this
	# script wrote for an agent an earlier image installed under the same
	# command — opencode moved from opencode-ai to @opencode/cli (ADR
	# 26-10-15-848 §7). It runs a program this image no longer ships, beside
	# launchers written for the one it does, so it goes, and the sandbox is
	# pinned as a new one would be.
	if [ -L "$link" ]; then
		case $(readlink "$link") in
		"$store"/*) rm -f "$link" ;;
		esac
	fi
	# Anything else already at the path — a real file, a directory, a link out
	# of the store — belongs to whoever put it there.
	if [ -e "$link" ] || [ -L "$link" ]; then
		return 0
	fi

	candidate=$(newest_version)
	[ -n "$candidate" ] || return 0
	image=$(image_version)
	if [ -z "$image" ]; then

		# cannot be decided. Leave the image's own copy on PATH: it is what the
		# box runs today, and preferring it cannot downgrade anybody. Failing
		# the other way pins whatever the cache happens to hold — and a cache
		# that lags a freshly bumped image is the normal state, so the box would
		# silently run an older agent for the rest of its life (ADR 0114 §2).
		return 0
	fi
	if ! newer_than "$candidate" "$image"; then
		# The image's own copy is at least as new, and it is already on PATH.
		return 0
	fi

	mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
	ln -sfn "$dir/$candidate/bin/$AGENT_BIN" "$link"
	touch_pin "$candidate"
}

# pinned_recently is true while some sandbox still says it is using a version.
pinned_recently() {
	[ -d "$dir/$1/pins" ] || return 1
	[ -n "$(find "$dir/$1/pins" -type f -mtime -"$pin_grace_days" 2>/dev/null | head -1)" ]
}

# prune enforces retention: the newest few versions always, anything a sandbox
# has touched recently, and nothing else. Without it the store grows by a
# quarter of a gigabyte per release.
#
# It walks every directory rather than every *version*, because the trees that
# most need deleting are the ones that are not versions: a tree whose own delete
# was interrupted has lost its executable, so a pass that iterated versions
# could never see it again, and it would hold its hundreds of megabytes forever.
prune() {
	# A version string holds no spaces, so a space-delimited haystack is enough
	# to ask "is this one of the ones we keep".
	keep=$(store_versions | sort -V | tail -n "$keep_versions" | tr '\n' ' ')
	for entry in "$dir"/*; do
		version=${entry##*/}
		case $version in
		'*' | .*) continue ;;
		esac
		[ -d "$dir/$version" ] || continue
		case " $keep " in
		*" $version "*) continue ;;
		esac
		if is_version "$version" && pinned_recently "$version"; then
			continue
		fi
		# Tolerated rather than trusted, and braced because this is an rm -rf.
		# touch_pin is the one writer that does not hold this lock — it runs in
		# every login, and holding a lock across somebody else's download would
		# be far worse — so it can create a file under a tree this is walking
		# and leave rm with ENOTEMPTY. Under `set -e` that would abort the whole
		# refresh, and for `upgrade` it would exit before re-pinning, silently.
		# What survives is a directory is_version refuses, which this pass
		# deletes the next time it runs.
		rm -rf "${dir:?}/${version:?}" 2>/dev/null || true
	done
	# Every fetch holds the lock this pass holds, and removes its own temporary
	# tree on every exit path, so a .tmp-* still here belongs to a fetch that was
	# killed — a sandbox powering itself off mid-download is ordinary
	# (ADR 0108). Age would only delay reclaiming it.
	for entry in "$dir"/.tmp-*; do
		[ -e "$entry" ] || continue
		rm -rf "$entry" 2>/dev/null || true
	done
}

# fetch installs one version into the store. The tree is built under a dot name
# and moved in with a single rename, so another sandbox either sees a complete
# version or no version at all.
fetch() {
	if is_version "$1"; then
		return 0
	fi
	# A directory under this name that is not a usable version is wreckage — an
	# interrupted delete, or an install that died after its rename. Clearing it
	# is what lets the store heal: asking `[ -d ]` here instead would skip the
	# fetch forever while nothing could ever pin the name. Safe under the lock
	# every writer takes, and for the same reason a stale .tmp of our own PID
	# (PIDs repeat across sandboxes) is only ever an orphan.
	rm -rf "${dir:?}/${1:?}" 2>/dev/null || true
	tmp=$dir/.tmp-$$
	rm -rf "$tmp"
	if ! timeout 1800 npm install -g --prefix "$tmp" "$AGENT_PACKAGE@$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		rm -rf "$tmp"
		return 1
	fi
	if [ ! -x "$tmp/bin/$AGENT_BIN" ]; then
		rm -rf "$tmp"
		return 1
	fi

	# *into* an existing directory, so a target that came back during the
	# install would bury the tree one level down, where is_version refuses it
	# and prune deletes it next pass — half an hour of download thrown away and
	# reported as a success. Half an hour is also why the clearing above is not
	# this check: touch_pin can recreate the name in between, and the early
	# `rm -rf` is allowed to fail quietly, which this one is not.
	if [ -e "$dir/$1" ] && ! rm -rf "${dir:?}/${1:?}"; then
		rm -rf "$tmp"
		return 1
	fi

		rm -rf "$tmp"
		return 1
	fi

	is_version "$1"

# exit status, because "nothing happened" has several causes and `upgrade` has
# to tell a person which one it hit:

#   windowed    the check window has not passed; the registry was not asked
#   busy        another sandbox holds the store lock
#   unreachable the registry did not answer

# refresh_latest is the version the registry named, for reporting it back.

			return 0

	# Stamped on the attempt, not on its success: the registry query is the
	# thing being rate-limited, and a sandbox with no way out should not ask
	# again at every login. A download that fails leaves the version absent,
	# and the next window fetches it.
	touch "$stamp"
	if [ -z "$latest" ]; then
		refresh_outcome=unreachable
		return 0
	fi

	refresh_latest=$latest
	if is_version "$latest"; then
		refresh_outcome=current
	elif ! worth_fetching "$latest"; then
		refresh_outcome=behind
	elif fetch "$latest"; then
		refresh_outcome=fetched
	else
		refresh_outcome=failed
	fi
	prune
}

cmd_upgrade() {
	was=$(pinned_version)
	[ -n "$was" ] || was=$(image_version)
	cmd_refresh force
	# Say which of these it was. Reporting "already the newest available" when
	# the registry was never reached is the one answer a person cannot act on,
	# and it is what every one of these used to print.
	case $refresh_outcome in
	busy)
		printf 'discobox: another sandbox is fetching a new %s; try again shortly.\n' "$AGENT_BIN" >&2
		return 1
		;;
	unreachable)
		printf 'discobox: could not reach the registry to look for a newer %s.\n' "$AGENT_BIN" >&2
		return 1
		;;
	failed)
		printf 'discobox: installing the newest %s failed; still on %s.\n' "$AGENT_BIN" "$was" >&2
		return 1
		;;
	behind)
		# Not a failure, and not "you are up to date" either: the registry is
		# publishing something older than this sandbox can already run.
		printf 'discobox: the registry publishes %s %s, which is not newer than the %s here; staying on %s.\n' \
			"$AGENT_BIN" "$refresh_latest" "$was" "$was"
		return 0
		;;
	esac
	# An upgrade is asked for, so unlike pin it replaces a pin this sandbox
	# already holds. A link it did not write is still left alone.
	if [ -n "$(pinned_version)" ]; then
		rm -f "$link"
	fi
	cmd_pin
	now=$(pinned_version)
	[ -n "$now" ] || now=$(image_version)
	if [ "$now" = "$was" ]; then
		printf 'discobox: %s is %s, already the newest available.\n' "$AGENT_BIN" "$now"
	else
		printf 'discobox: %s upgraded from %s to %s.\n' "$AGENT_BIN" "$was" "$now"
		printf 'discobox: restart %s for it to take effect.\n' "$AGENT_BIN"
	fi
}

cmd_status() {
	printf 'package: %s\n' "$AGENT_PACKAGE"
	printf 'image:   %s\n' "$(image_version)"
	printf 'pinned:  %s\n' "$(pinned_version)"
	printf 'store:   %s\n' "$dir"
	store_versions | sort -V | sed 's/^/  /'
}

case ${1-} in
pin)
	cmd_pin
	;;
refresh)
	if [ "${2-}" = --force ]; then
		cmd_refresh force
	else
		cmd_refresh window
	fi
	;;
upgrade)
	cmd_upgrade
	;;
status)
	cmd_status
	;;
*)
	usage >&2
	exit 2
	;;
esac

`claude` is installed in that box, but the user the box runs as can't reach it. The box is a boxd machine (`dvm-pool-…`). Its base image keeps Node and Claude in the `boxd` user's home, while the box runs as `darren` (uid 1002), who isn't allowed into that home.

**The chain**

1. The base image installed Node with nvm under `/home/boxd/.nvm/...`. It then made `/usr/local/bin/node`, `npm` and `claude` symlinks into `/home/boxd`.
2. `/home/boxd` is `drwxr-x--- boxd:boxd`. `darren` isn't in the `boxd` group, so all three symlinks are broken for `darren`. Even `ls /home/boxd/.local/bin` gets "Permission denied".
3. The harness's `install-cli.sh` did run. It ran as root and did `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Root's `npm` is that same `/usr/local/bin/npm` symlink into boxd's nvm, so Claude 2.1.316 went to `/home/boxd/.nvm/versions/node/v24.22.1/lib/node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-code`. Those files are owned by root and readable, but they sit behind the locked `/home/boxd`.
4. The backup copy didn't help either. The pool-cached agent store does have 2.1.316 at `~/.local/share/discobox/agents/anthropic-ai-claude-code/2.1.316`. But `discobox-agent-store status` shows `image:` empty. That's because `image_version` only looks in `/usr/lib/node_modules` and `/usr/local/lib/node_modules`, and neither has Claude. The pin step then deliberately does nothing when it can't read the image's version, so `~/.local/bin/claude` was never created.

So `discobox-harness-run` runs `exec claude`, finds nothing it can execute, and you're left at the login shell. That's also why the box's name is the shell prompt title (`darren@dvm-pool-…`).

**How to fix it properly**, most targeted first:
- **Let `darren` through `/home/boxd`** when the boxd pool sets up its machine: `chmod o+x /home/boxd` is enough. This is the smallest change, and it fixes `node` and `npm` too, which are just as broken for `darren`.
- **Stop installing harnesses through whatever `npm` root happens to find.** `install-cli.sh` could install into a fixed prefix such as `--prefix /usr/local`, and the agent store's `image_version` could ask `npm root -g` instead of using a hardcoded list. Then a base image that puts Node in a user's home can't hide the harness.
- Or run boxd boxes as `boxd`. That probably conflicts with the uid mapping the box uses for `darren`, so I'd rather not.

**Quick unblock for this box** (I haven't run either; say if you want me to):
```sh
discobox shell sbx_yhg7pcs4by9bmsq5 -- sudo chmod o+x /home/boxd
# or point darren at the store copy:
discobox shell sbx_yhg7pcs4by9bmsq5 -- sh -c 'mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -sfn ~/.local/share/discobox/agents/anthropic-ai-claude-code/2.1.316/bin/claude ~/.local/bin/claude'
```

Either way, restart the box afterwards so Claude starts.
I think #2 is the best fix, stop install harnesss through whatever dir it finds. Can we do an audit of everything else to make sure that there aren't other similar pathing issues in our bundles?

Everything else is a **feature** — `node`, `docker`, `browser`, `desktop`,
`nix`, `brew`, `go`, `python`, `rust`, `bun`, `mise`, `build`, `cli`,

  reachability from a system PATH by every user, and writability where
  Discobox needs it. boxd's `/usr/local/bin/node`, a link into one user's nvm,

  runtime integration in the box reads that rather than probing (0145 §3

  launchers, session-bus drop-ins, the desktop API) become conditional on it.
  The manifest's `features` stays the authored declaration of what a bundle
  provides, and the document stays the pool agent's to write (0012 §§2, 8):
  an outcome the box observed is not written into it.
- **A reported feature grants nothing.** The pool and the server never decide
  access — the pool's builder or registry among it — from what a box reports
  it has; the box would be choosing its own access.

Exit code 1 # Provision Design How a box is provisioned from its features ([ADR 26-10-16-423](../../docs/adr/26-10-16-423-a-harness-is-a-provisioning-bundle-and-the-agent-provisions-any-box.md) §§3–6). What a feature's `provision.yaml` may say, and the `provision.json` document, are the root [`provisionspec`](../../pkg/provisionspec) contract; this package is what is done with them. ## Steps A feature's steps are the runner's typed kinds: `file` (with `merge: json`, an RFC 7396 merge patch over the file the box already has, which is refused rather than replaced when it is not a JSON object, so a provider's `daemon.json` keeps what ours does not set; its `restart` names the units that read the file only as they start), `systemd` (enable, mask, drop-in, through `systemctl`), `group` (asked of `runuser`, then `groupadd`), `env` (a `/etc/profile.d/zz-discobox---.sh` script, named to sort after the box's own profile scripts so one that sets PATH outright does not drop it, which also puts its `path` ahead of `/usr/local/bin`'s shims; it reaches login shells only, never an exec that gets the manifest's env; a feature's scripts no step selecting the box still writes are removed with their records), `download` (fetched through the environment's proxy, given up after a minute without a byte, and moved into place only once its sha256 matches; with `unpack`, a gzipped tar or a zip, told apart by its first bytes, unpacked beside its directory and swapped in whole, refusing an entry or link that would land outside it, and a zip whose entries carry no Unix modes), `packages` (`apt-get`, keeping a configuration file already in a package's way rather than asking; a list per distribution, the box's own os-release `ID`'s, else the first `ID_LIKE`'s that has one, and a box no list names fails the step), and `run` (whose `inputs` name the files and directories its script reads beside itself, so the digest covers them), each selected by `os`, `arch` and os-release `ID`/`ID_LIKE`. On a booted box (`Runner.Booted`, systemd running: a box's boot and a snapshot's, never an image's build) an enabled unit is started, and a unit a step places a drop-in for, or a file names in `restart`, is restarted if it is running (`systemctl try-restart`), once, after the feature's steps, all in one call so systemd orders them (`Step.Restarts`): it read them as it started, and the box may have started it before the feature was provisioned — containerd and a socket-activated dockerd are up before the `docker` feature lays their drop-ins — so it would otherwise run without them until the next boot. Each step is keyed by a digest of its definition and every file it names, recorded under `/opt/discobox/provision/steps/` on the root filesystem, never a declared volume; a step whose record matches is skipped unless its `check` exits non-zero (drift), so a second run changes nothing. A box that is not Linux of the Debian family is refused by name before any step runs, unless it has no features to provision. ## Who runs it | Caller | Entry | Runs | |---|---|---| | The agent, every boot | `Boot(…, wireOnly=false)` → `Runner.Provision` | Everything, with `Background`: the server answers meanwhile | | `boot.Wire` / `boot.Provision` | `Boot(…, wireOnly=true)` → `Runner.Wire` | Wiring alone, before the account exists | | `discobox-sandbox-agent snapshot` | `Snapshot` → `Runner.Provision` with `Snapshot` | Every step blocking, the plan's features off, and what a feature keeps out of a snapshot `Deferred`: a box provisioned as a snapshot is taken ([Snapshots](#snapshots)) | | `discobox-provision apply`, on a pool | `Pool` → `Runner.Provision` | Every feature of the pool's bundles, every step blocking, nothing off and no placeholders: nothing runs on a pool but what its bundles lay ([ADR 26-10-24-953](../../docs/adr/26-10-24-953-every-box-is-provisioned-from-an-ordered-list-of-bundles-and-a-pool-is-a-box.md) §2) | At boot the trees are the box's pins' bundles, in the pins' order (`bundlestore.Trees`, handed to `BootPlan`): a sandbox's sandbox bundle and then its harness's, or a pool's pool bundle. Each is read at its stable link in the content store, `agentlayer.BundleTree(name)`, pointed at the pin's tree before the run starts, so the paths a step or a link names stay the same across upgrades and follow the trees; a step's record keys its feature's directory too, so one applied from another path is applied again. Every feature's directory moved when the trees came to be linked by name, so the first start of a box made before on a new agent runs every step once more, which they are idempotent for (ADR 26-10-24-953, Consequences). Nothing says which tree is which ([ADR 26-10-24-953](../../docs/adr/26-10-24-953-every-box-is-provisioned-from-an-ordered-list-of-bundles-and-a-pool-is-a-box.md) §1): order is the tie-break of what runs first, a later bundle's blocking features after an earlier one's, and what blocks is each feature's own `async`. A step that lays a binary the build made links it from the tree rather than copying it, so a new agent is a new file and no step applied again. A box with no trees has no features: `provision.json` lists none, and its tools are its image's. Opt-outs are the bootstrap's `features` (`sandbox.json`), which the client read from the repository's `.discobox/settings.json`. Core's steps never lay the agent's own units: they boot a box before any feature is provisioned, so they are root `agentlayer`'s, placed by the pool with the agent. ## A run ```mermaid flowchart TD plan["plan: order by requires,
probe adopt, decide off"] -->|refused| fail["readiness failed"] plan --> wire["wiring of every feature on:
group and env steps"] wire --> ph["placeholders for features
left to the background"] ph --> block["blocking steps in requires order:
every feature not async, what they require"] block --> ready["readiness decided
(Tracker.AwaitReady)"] ready --> bg["the rest, in parallel,
each after what it requires"] bg --> done["provision.json: ready or failed"] ``` - **Outcome.** A feature turned off, and required by nothing, is `off`: no step runs and its env scripts go, but nothing is uninstalled. One requiring an `off` feature is off too. A feature that is not `async`, or that one requires, is refused when turned off, naming both — unless its `adopt` check passes. Core (`provisionspec.Core`) is never off: the server refuses it in a create's `features`, and a run refuses it outright. - **Adopted.** `adopt` is checked by the agent, not a script: each command on `SystemPath`, run by every user, never in a home directory, never the agent's own personality or a placeholder; the version floor; the writable paths. Adopted skips the `install: true` steps and applies the rest. A feature with a record of an install step is ours and is never adopted. - **How.** Ready is `adopted`, `installed` when this run applied a step, else `snapshot`. - **Blocking.** Every feature that is not `async` — core, a harness's features; the platform's optional features are `async` — and *whole*: everything a blocking feature requires, every step, its `async` marks overridden, since a blocking feature needs all of what it requires. In a blocking feature a step marked `async` defers itself and every step after it, so steps still run in the order written. Without `Background` every step blocks. - **Failure.** A failed step is not recorded, fails its feature and those requiring it, and nothing else. A failure before readiness fails it, and its error names each failed feature's log. - **Locks.** `packages` steps and `run` steps marked `apt` take one lock; a `file` step with `merge: json` takes another across its read and its write, so features merging into one file in parallel keep each other's keys. Npm install scripts use a private temporary cache and remove only that cache. They run while a box provisions, at its boot or as a snapshot is taken, when the user's npm cache can be a mounted, pool-shared volume; provisioning must not clear or remove it. ## Snapshots A snapshot is a box provisioned for no sandbox, and kept so a box of the same plan starts from it (ADR 26-10-16-423 §8). Mark what must be each box's own: anything keyed to the machine, or provisioned fresh on purpose. `snapshot` is not part of a step's digest (`StepDigest`): it says when the step runs, not what it does. ## Its state `Tracker` holds the document, replaces `provision.json` whole on each change, and is what the agent's gates and status report read. Terminals use `AwaitReady`; declared services use `AwaitFeatures`, waiting for either their named features or, by default, the full run, including async features. Status updates wake feature waiters without polling. A required feature's failure or explicit opt-out prevents launch; the default ignores opt-outs. Each feature's steps write to `/var/log/discobox/provision/.log`. ## Placeholders A feature left to the background has each of its `commands` written to `PlaceholderDir`, last on every PATH (the image's PATH, and a profile script the run writes when it writes one). A placeholder execs `discobox-provision run FEATURE COMMAND`, which says on stderr that it waits, waits on `provision.json`, then finds the real command past the placeholders and execs it. content.text:
That error comes from a different gap in the same family. The box sets `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR=/var/lib/claude-code` (from the harness's `image.json`) and declares that path a data volume owned by the box user. On a machine box like boxd, `boot.Provision` wires no declared volumes, and nothing else creates the directory either. So Claude can't make it, because `/var/lib` belongs to root. It's the only declared volume outside your home that's missing; the missing ones under `~` are harmless.

To unblock this box:
```sh
discobox shell sbx_yhg7pcs4by9bmsq5 -- sudo install -d -o darren -g darren -m 0700 /var/lib/claude-code
```
Then run `discobox-harness-run` again. Your `chmod o+x /home/boxd` also means boxd's own `node` and `codex` now win on PATH over ours. That works, but it's not what the box is supposed to run.

## Audit: install paths and command lookups in our bundles

I read every feature's `provision.yaml` and scripts, and checked how each command resolves on this box for both `darren` and root.

**Root cause for the Node tools.** Our adopt check (`sandbox-agent/provision/adopt.go`) is correct: it refuses boxd's nvm `node` because it lives in a user's home. So the node feature installs NodeSource Node into `/usr/bin`. But the box's refused copies stay in `/usr/local/bin` (`node`, `npm`, `npx`, `corepack`), which comes before `/usr/bin` on everyone's PATH. Every later step and launcher calls `node` or `npm` by bare name, so they get the box's copy, not ours. That would also be true of an old Node that failed only the version check, not the home check.

| # | Where | What goes wrong | Seen on this box |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `install-cli.sh` in all 6 harnesses | `npm install -g` puts the CLI wherever the box's npm points, which here is boxd's home | yes: Claude went into `/home/boxd/.nvm/...` |
| 2 | `node/install-pnpm.sh` | same `npm install -g` problem | yes: `pnpm` isn't installed for anyone |
| 3 | `node/agent-store` | `image_version` only looks in two hardcoded folders, so it found no version and refused to pin; `fetch`/`refresh` also use bare `npm` | yes: `image:` was empty |
| 4 | Every harness's `capture.sh` and `configure.sh`, plus `codex-cli/launch.sh` and `opencode/model.sh` | they run bare `node`, so they get the box's Node, which may be one the version check rejected | now yes, since `/home/boxd` is open |
| 5 | The box's own `/usr/local/bin/claude` and `/usr/local/bin/codex` links | they come before wherever we install the harness CLI, so even a correctly installed `claude` loses to boxd's 2.1.309 or a broken link | yes |
| 6 | `rust/install-rustup.sh` | runs as root with no `CARGO_HOME`, so rustup lands in `/root/.cargo` and the box user never gets `rustup` or `cargo` | yes: neither exists for `darren`. This doesn't depend on boxd, so it likely affects every box |
| 7 | Declared volumes on machine boxes | paths outside the home, like `/var/lib/claude-code`, are never created | yes: the error you just hit |
| 8 | `python/install-uv.sh` (low confidence) | it installs into `/usr/local/bin`; if a box had a `uv` link into a home there, the installer might write through it | no, not seen here |

**These are fine:** `go` (its own `/usr/local/go`, earlier on PATH), `bun` (overwrites `/usr/local`), `brew`, and the apt-installed tools (`mise`, `gh`, `direnv`). `shells-editors` is the model to copy: it downloads into a folder we own under `/usr/local/lib/discobox/...` and links each command into `/usr/local/bin`.

In a Docker pool, the sandbox lives in a container the pool made, and the pool agent has mounted its config volume. At boot the sandbox agent runs `Wire`. A machine box (boxd, or our own VMs) boots its own init, and has no pool-mounted volumes and no config volume. ## Decision

### 1. The sandbox agent does not assume it is PID 1

It is an ordinary service of the guest's own init. When it starts and its
bootstrap is not there yet, it **waits for it** — on every OS, built into the
agent — rather than exiting or being skipped. It then provisions what applies
outside a container — the sandbox user and its groups, the home skeleton,
`~/.gitconfig` and direnv config — and serves. Declared volumes are not wired
(0126 §2); sources and everything dynamic arrive through the intake as they do
on every backend (26-10-08-127 §1).

On a systemd image the wait is also expressed natively: a `.path` unit
(`PathExists=` on the bootstrap) activates the agent's service, so a machine
with no sandbox in it runs no agent. launchd and the SCM start the agent at
boot, and it waits.

A container keeps its PID-1 `init` flow; this decision does not change it.

### 2. A VM backend's contract is start, place the bootstrap, and one address

The pool asks a VM backend for three things, in order:

1. **Start the machine** from an image that has the sandbox agent installed.
2. **Place `sandbox.json`** at the agent's fixed path, through the running
   guest. This is 0126 §3's bootstrap exception, moved from before boot to
   before the agent: the agent is not running yet, so the pool still changes
   nothing inside a running sandbox except by asking it.
3. **Return one address that reaches the agent's API.** It exists from create,
   answers once the agent serves, and stays the same across stop and start.

The backend exposes no other guest port and offers no exec or file operations
to the pool. Which guest port is the agent's is the image's to declare, not
the backend's to know.

### 3. A provider's public HTTPS is an acceptable address

For a provider-hosted VM (boxd, exe.dev), the address is the provider's HTTPS
URL for the agent's port. It is 0126 §5's "address the pool can dial", and it
is public: **the sandbox agent's own token check is the only gate**, which §5
already makes the authorization decision on every transport. Two things follow:

- A route the agent answers without a token is answered to the internet, so
  the agent's unauthenticated surface must be audited and kept minimal before a
  provider-hosted backend is enabled.
- The provider terminates TLS and sees the traffic. It runs the machine, so it
  is already inside the sandbox's trust boundary; but transport-level client
  authentication (mTLS between pool and agent) cannot ride this hop.

A provider feature that restricts who can reach the URL — boxd's tailnet-only
mode, or anything like it — is welcome hardening, never a substitute for the
token check.

A local VM's address is the host-to-guest socket of ADR 0144: vsock on
Virtualization.framework, hvsocket on Hyper-V.

  `tcp/attach` and `udp/attach` already reach every port from inside the
  sandbox, behind its tokens.

## Deferred

- **Containers on the same model** — systemd as PID 1, the agent waiting for
  its bootstrap, provisioning moved out of `init`. Revisit when the PID-1 flow
  is the only thing a container still needs that a VM does not: declared
  volumes are the reason it exists today.
- **Egress confinement on provider VMs** (0126 §6) is not decided here. boxd
  documents a per-machine egress allowlist enforced outside the machine, which
  a restored machine starts without; a boxd backend is not enabled until it is
  set on every create and restore, and verified.
- **Reaching the pool from a provider VM** (0126 §§6–7): a pool the provider's
  machines cannot reach cannot serve them. Where the pool runs is the operator's
  choice and outside this decision.

## Consequences

- sandbox-agent waits for its bootstrap instead of being skipped without it,
  and gains a provisioning path that runs as a service rather than as PID 1.
- The sandbox image replaces the agent unit's `ConditionPathExists` with a
  `discobox-sandbox-agent.path` unit.
- disco-vm's driver contract narrows to lifecycle, guest file and exec
  operations for its own builds and the bootstrap, and one service endpoint per
  instance, from a port the image declares.
- The pool gains a VM backend that is the three steps of §2, plus the intake
  over the returned address.
## Decision

### 1. systemd is PID 1 in a container

The sandbox image's entrypoint is its init. `discobox-sandbox-agent init` is
removed, with the exec plan behind it: there is no compatibility entrypoint,
and an image built FROM an older base keeps the older agent it was built with.

A bare `docker run <image> bash` therefore boots systemd rather than a login
shell as the sandbox user. A debug session overrides the entrypoint.

### 2. A unit of the image wires the sandbox before `sysinit.target`

`discobox-wire.service` runs the agent's provisioning with wiring on — the
config volume onto `/etc/discobox`, the secrets volume onto
`/run/discobox/secrets`, the declared volumes, the sources, and the user
provisioning 26-10-09-143 §1 lists. It is:

- **Conditional on the config volume's bootstrap**, which only a pool's
  container has. Without it the unit is skipped, not failed: a bare container
  boots with no sandbox in it, as a VM with no bootstrap does.
- **Ordered before, and required by, `sysinit.target`**, and before
  `systemd-tmpfiles-setup.service`. Every unit with default dependencies starts
  after `sysinit.target`, so nothing that uses a wired path — Docker,
  containerd, the Nix daemon, the user's session, the agent — can start ahead
  of the wiring, and tmpfiles creates nothing underneath a mount.
- **Run on every boot.** A container's mounts do not survive a restart, and its
  account does not survive a rebuild, while `/var/lib/discobox` — where a VM
  records that it was provisioned — is a data volume that survives both. That
  record does not gate a container: what `init` did on every boot, the unit
  does on every boot.

The agent's own start is unchanged. `discobox-sandbox-agent.path` fires once
the unit has bound the bootstrap into place, and the agent's `Provision` finds
the config volume and does nothing, as it does today after `init`.

### 3. The identity comes from the bootstrap

The unit resolves the sandbox user from `sandbox.json`'s `user`, as the VM path
does. A unit does not see the container's environment, and the bootstrap is the
same manifest layer `DISCOBOX_USER_*` is rendered from (ADR 0012). The export
container keeps reading the environment, which the pool agent renders from
that same bootstrap (ADR 0129); it has no unit, so nothing changes for it.

### 4. Units bound to the sandbox user are reloaded, on every backend

The session-bus and desktop drop-ins name the sandbox user, which only the
bootstrap knows, so they cannot be in the image. `init` wrote them before
systemd read its units. The unit writes them and reloads the manager — what the
VM path already does after its provisioning — so one sequence serves both.

### 5. A wiring failure ends the container

A sandbox whose wiring failed must not run: every service would write its
state — the home, `/var/lib/docker` — into the image layer, where a rebuild
discards it. Two things make that impossible rather than unlikely:

- `sysinit.target` requires the unit, so its failure fails the target and
  nothing behind it starts.
- The unit's failure action is the manager's exit, with a non-zero status. The
  container stops, as it did when `init` returned an error, and the pool agent
  reports it the way it reports any exited sandbox: the exit code and the tail
  of the container's log. The unit therefore logs to the console as well as the
  journal, which does not outlive the container.

The pool agent sets no restart policy on a sandbox container, so a persistent
failure is one stopped sandbox with a reason, not a loop.

# Architecture Decision Records

An ADR records a decision, the alternatives rejected, and why — at the time it
was made.

## When to write one

Only when either is true:

- A plausible alternative was rejected for a non-obvious reason.
- Something was deferred with a specific condition for revisiting it.

Otherwise skip the ADR and update the relevant `DESIGN.md`. Most changes do not
need one.

## Rules

- **Immutable.** Never edit an accepted ADR. Superseded by a new one that links
  back; mark the old one `Superseded by <id>`. An ADR's ID is as immutable as
  its text — never renumber one.
- **Outside the drill-down hierarchy.** ADRs live here, never next to code.
  `DESIGN.md`/`REVIEW.md` are read root-down by agents on every task; ADRs are
  not, and must not be, because they are history rather than current state.
- **Not a substitute for `DESIGN.md`.** When the work lands, update the live
  design docs to describe what now exists. The ADR keeps the "why we didn't";
  `DESIGN.md` keeps the "what is".

## Status lifecycle

`Proposed` → `Accepted` → (`Superseded by <id>`)

Use `Rejected` for decisions considered and declined; keep the file.

## Identifiers

An ADR's ID is `YY-MM-DD-RRR` — the date it was written, plus three random
decimal digits ([ADR 26-09-24-458](26-09-24-458-adr-ids-are-a-date-and-a-random-suffix.md)).
It is generated, never allocated from a sequence, so two branches in flight
cannot claim the same one.

```bash
python3 -c "import secrets; print(f'{secrets.randbelow(1000):03d}')"
```

- Filename `YY-MM-DD-RRR-<slug>.md`, heading `# YY-MM-DD-RRR — Title`, cited in
  prose and code comments as `ADR 26-09-24-458` or `ADR 26-09-24-458 §3`.
- The date is fixed when the file is created. Where it and the `Date` header
  disagree — an ADR written before a long review — the header is authoritative.
- If two branches somehow draw the same ID, **re-roll the suffix** on one of
  them. Nothing outside that branch cites it yet, and no value is the "correct"
  one to fight over.
- ADRs `0001`–`0149` predate this scheme and keep their four-digit numbers,
  which are cited across the tree. Both forms are permanent; the old ones sort
  first.

## Workflow

Nygard-style ADRs (see adr.github.io) combined with current-state design docs:

# 26-11-02-023 — A machine sandbox wires its declared volumes from its own data and cache roots

- **Status**: Proposed
- **Date**: 2026-11-02
- **Amends**:
  [0126](0126-a-sandbox-does-not-share-a-host-or-a-filesystem-with-its-pool.md)
  §2's "where it has none, the declared-volume mechanism does not apply at
  all"; [26-10-09-143](26-10-09-143-a-vm-sandbox-starts-its-agent-when-its-bootstrap-arrives.md)
  §1's "Declared volumes are not wired"; and
  [26-10-10-767](26-10-10-767-a-container-sandbox-boots-systemd-and-a-unit-wires-its-volumes.md)
  §2's unit conditional on a config volume "which only a pool's container
  has".
- **Relates to**: [0007](0007-declarative-sandbox-volumes-wired-by-the-sandbox-agent.md),
  [0094](0094-the-pool-cache-is-partitioned-by-the-sandbox-users-uid.md),
  [26-10-16-423](26-10-16-423-a-harness-is-a-provisioning-bundle-and-the-agent-provisions-any-box.md),
  [26-10-27-345](26-10-27-345-a-machine-sandbox-is-made-again-in-place-and-its-bootstrap-names-where-its-agent-listens.md)
  and discobox-ai/vm#23.

## Context

A harness and the platform declare volumes (ADR 0007): paths such as `%HOME%`,
`/var/lib/docker`, `~/.cache` and Claude Code's `/var/lib/claude-code`, each
`data` or `cache`, with an owner and a mode. In a Docker sandbox the pool
mounts `/.discobox/data` and `/.discobox/cache`, and `discobox-wire.service`
(26-10-10-767) binds or overlays each declared path from them before anything
uses it. That is also what *creates* each path, owned by whoever the
declaration says.

A machine sandbox (boxd, or a local VM through disco-vm) skips all of it. 0126
§2 said the declared-volume mechanism does not apply where there is no PID-1
flow, and the wire unit is conditional on a config volume no machine has. So
on a machine:

- **A declared path nothing else creates does not exist.** Claude Code's
  harness sets `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR=/var/lib/claude-code` and declares it a
  `data` volume owned by the sandbox user; on a boxd sandbox `claude` fails
  with `EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/var/lib/claude-code'`. Every path a
  harness declares outside the home has the same gap.
- **A box has two layouts.** What a sandbox keeps is spread across its disk on
  a machine and gathered under `/.discobox/data` in a container. Clearing the
  cache, a box's own skill about where things persist, the verify recipes and
  any future export each have to know which kind of box they are on.
- **A machine's durable tree cannot be separated from its disk.** 26-10-27-345
  rebuilds a machine in place because its data *is* its disk; a data volume of
  its own (discobox-ai/vm#23) would need the data to already live in one place
  to be moved onto it.

## Decision

### 1. A machine has `/.discobox/data` and `/.discobox/cache`

A Linux machine sandbox has both roots, as directories on its own disk. Every
declared volume is wired from them exactly as in a container: the same
`volumeDir` layout (data per target, cache partitioned by uid under
`.users/<uid>`, a `scope: shared` path at the cache root), a bind for an empty
target, an overlay for a data target the box already has content at, the
owner and mode the declaration names, parents before children.

The cache stays private to the box (0126 §2 stands): nothing outside the
machine shares it. Its uid partition is kept anyway, so the layout is one
layout and a machine's cache can later move to a shared volume without a
re-seed. Source-scoped pool data (`/.discobox/data-per-source`) stays
unavailable on a machine, as 0126 §2 says.

When disco-vm gives an instance a volume (discobox-ai/vm#23), the roots are
where it mounts. Nothing else changes: the wiring reads directories, not
devices.

### 2. The same unit wires both, before `sysinit.target`, on every boot

`discobox-wire.service` runs on a machine too. Its condition becomes "this box
has a sandbox": the config volume's bootstrap in a container, the placed
bootstrap at `/etc/discobox/sandbox.json` on a machine. It keeps its ordering
(before `local-fs.target`, `sysinit.target` and tmpfiles), so nothing that
uses a wired path — the provider's own Docker on boxd among it — starts ahead
of the wiring, and it runs on every boot, since a machine's mounts do not
survive a restart either.

What a machine has no volume for is not wired: its config stays the placed
bootstrap, its secrets and sources keep arriving through the intake
(26-10-08-127). The unit wires the sandbox user and the declared volumes; on a
container it also binds config, secrets and sources, as today.

A wiring failure must not let the box run, on either kind: in a container the
manager exits (26-10-10-767 §5); on a machine it powers off, which the pool
reports as a stopped sandbox, the way it reports an exited container.

### 3. A machine's first placement restarts it before anything runs

A machine boots before its bootstrap is placed, so its own services — boxd's
dockerd and containerd — are already running on the paths the wiring would
mount over. The first placement therefore places the bootstrap and the agent
layer, starts nothing, and restarts the machine; the wire unit then runs at
its first real boot, before those services, and the agent and feature
provisioning start after it. Placement already restarts a machine whose
placed bootstrap moved (26-10-27-345); a first placement becomes one more
reason to.

A machine provisioned before this decision is wired at its next start. Its
existing content at a declared data path — the home, `/var/lib/docker` — is
non-empty, so it is overlaid, not hidden: it stays as the lower layer and new
writes go to `/.discobox/data`.

## Alternatives rejected

- **Only create each declared path, owned as declared, without mounting.**
  The smallest fix for `/var/lib/claude-code`. Rejected because it keeps two
  layouts: the gap it closes is one symptom of a machine's durable tree having
  no single place, and every consumer of that tree (cache clearing, export,
  a data volume) would still need a machine branch.
- **Wire on a live machine, stopping and restarting the units that use the
  wired paths.** Avoids the first-boot restart. Rejected because the pool
  cannot know every unit of a provider's image that holds a declared path
  open, and a mount laid under a running process splits its view of the path
  silently rather than failing.
- **Have each feature create its paths in its own provisioning steps.**
  A declared volume's owner is the sandbox user's uid, which a snapshot shared
  by every box cannot bake in, and it would duplicate in each feature what the
  declaration already says.

## Deferred

- **Exporting and importing a machine sandbox's tree.** Still refused
  (`ErrUnsupported`). This decision makes `/.discobox/data` the tree to
  export, as in a container; revisit when a machine pool needs export.
- **A machine's data on a volume of its own**, and with it rebuilding a
  machine rather than reusing its disk (26-10-27-345): revisit when disco-vm
  gives an instance a volume (discobox-ai/vm#23).

## Consequences

- `boot.Provision` no longer skips volumes on a machine; the wiring moves to
  the unit on both kinds, and `Provision`'s once-per-sandbox record keeps the
  account and seeding steps it alone does.
- `discobox-wire.service`'s condition and failure action differ by box kind,
  and the agent layer the pool places on a machine already carries the unit.
- The machine runtime's first placement restarts the machine before the agent
  starts, adding one guest boot to a machine sandbox's create.
- The sandbox's `discobox` skill and the verify recipes describe one layout.
- A machine's `/.discobox/data` and the disk content it overlays both hold
  data; clearing a box's cache and reasoning about its disk use account for
  the lower layer a pre-existing machine keeps.

I've drafted the ADR as `Proposed`, since this reverses ADR 0126 §2: it currently says a machine gets no declared volumes at all. Per the repo's process, it needs your sign-off before any implementation. Nothing is committed yet.

The draft is `docs/adr/26-11-02-023-a-machine-sandbox-wires-its-declared-volumes-from-its-own-data-and-cache-roots.md`, and I added a `Proposed` row to `docs/adr/README.md`.

**What it decides**
1. **A Linux machine has `/.discobox/data` and `/.discobox/cache` on its own disk.** Declared volumes are wired from them exactly as in Docker: same folder layout, same per-uid cache split, bind for an empty path, overlay where the box already has content. The cache stays private to the machine. When disco-vm gives machines a separate volume (discobox-ai/vm#23), it just mounts at those roots.
2. **The same `discobox-wire.service` runs on both**, still before `sysinit.target` and on every boot. On a machine its trigger becomes the placed `/etc/discobox/sandbox.json` instead of the config volume. Config, secrets and sources keep arriving the way they do on a machine today. If wiring fails, a container exits as now and a machine powers off, so the pool reports it as stopped.
3. **The first placement restarts the machine before anything runs.** A machine is already up, with boxd's own `dockerd` and `containerd` running, by the time its bootstrap arrives. Mounting under them would be unsafe. So the first placement only places files and restarts, and wiring then happens at the next boot before those services start. Placement already restarts a machine when its bootstrap changes, so this reuses that.

**Costs to be aware of**
- **One extra reboot per machine create.**
- **Existing machines get wired at their next start.** Their current home and `/var/lib/docker` contents are kept: they become the read-only bottom layer, and new writes go to `/.discobox/data`.

**Rejected alternatives**
- **Just create the paths (my earlier #5).** It fixes `/var/lib/claude-code` but keeps two layouts.
- **Wire a live machine and restart the affected services.** The pool can't know every service in a provider's image that has those paths open.
- **Let each feature create its own paths.** A shared snapshot can't bake in each user's uid.

**Deferred:** exporting a machine's tree (now just `/.discobox/data`), and keeping a machine's data on its own volume.

The PATH fixes from the audit are separate and still waiting on your go-ahead. Once you accept the ADR, I'll commit it on its own and then implement it with the `DESIGN.md` updates. Do you want any changes to the draft first, especially the power-off on a failed wiring or the first-boot restart?

## Sandbox DNS

A sandbox is on its pool's internal network only, where Docker's embedded
resolver answers container names but forwards nothing else, so without help
no external name resolves
([ADR 0148](../docs/adr/0148-a-sandbox-resolves-names-through-its-pool-over-mtls.md)).

Plain DNS on that network would be answerable by any sandbox that claimed the
pool's address — every sandbox is root in a privileged container on the same
segment — so it travels the way the proxy and the credentials endpoint do:
over TLS, authenticated both ways by the pool's certificates.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    app["sandbox process"] -->|"127.0.0.11"| docker["Docker embedded DNS"]
    docker -->|"container names"| app
    docker -->|"everything else, to 169.254.53.53 on lo"| stub["sandbox proxy bridge (dnsstub)"]
    nested["nested-Docker container"] -->|"169.254.53.53, over a nested bridge"| stub
    stub -->|"DNS over TLS, client cert = sandbox"| fwd["proxy unit :17085 (dnsforward)"]
    fwd -->|"UDP, TCP on truncation"| up["pool's resolver"]
```

- `sandboxruntime` creates each sandbox container with the DNS server
  `proxyagent.SandboxDNSAddress` (`169.254.53.53`). It is the sandbox's own:
  the stub claims it on the sandbox's loopback, so Docker's resolver, which
  forwards from inside the sandbox's network namespace, delivers locally and
  nothing crosses the network in the clear. It drops anything for that address
  arriving on the pool's network (`eth+`, or a machine's `en+`), which a
  neighbor could otherwise route there. The sandbox's `nameserver` stays `127.0.0.11`, so container
  names resolve as before. The sandbox's nested Docker names the same address
  for its own containers ([ADR 26-10-15-760](../docs/adr/26-10-15-760-nested-docker-containers-resolve-through-the-sandboxs-stub.md)).
- The stub's two settings are in `bridge.json` beside the credentials endpoint,
  since all three reach the pool with the same keypair: `dnsListenAddress` (that
  address, port 53 — the sandbox's own, `sandboxconfig.SandboxDNSListenAddress`)
  and `dnsServer` (`https://discobox-pool-proxy:17085`, a wire URL like every
  other pool endpoint, from the bootstrap's pool endpoints; a bare `host:port`
  from an older bootstrap is TCP). The sandbox's intake renders the file.
- The proxy unit serves `dnsforward` on `0.0.0.0:17085` with the server
  configuration it shares with the credentials endpoint (`sandboxTLSConfig`),
  and answers from the first `nameserver` in the pool container's
  `resolv.conf` — Docker's embedded resolver, which forwards because the pool
  is also on a network with a route out. Its failing is logged and does not
  stop the proxy. Connections are capped in total and per source address at
  accept, before any handshake, since the process also carries every
  sandbox's egress; and per sandbox after it, by certificate name. The tunnel
  listener's own source is not capped as one: it splices every sandbox
  behind an edge ([Pools Behind An Edge](#pools-behind-an-edge)).
- The upstream is the pool's own resolver, so a sandbox can resolve the names
  of containers on the pool's egress network too. It cannot reach them.
- The server relays messages and decides nothing: DNS is not subject to the
  proxy's allowlist. It does decode each exchange — the name and type asked,
  the rcode, the answers' addresses and targets, or why there was no answer —
  and records it through the proxy's `RecordDNS` under the sandbox its
  certificate names, into the same trail, queue and retention as its HTTP.
  `audit/dns` relays it like `audit/http`, narrowed the same way.

**What's on `sbx_yhg7pcs4by9bmsq5`**

| | |
|---|---|
| DNS stub (`169.254.53.53:53`) | running; `dig @169.254.53.53 github.com` answers `140.82.121.4`, so the encrypted path to the pool works |
| `/etc/resolv.conf` | `nameserver 10.40.0.1`, boxd's resolver |

So any ordinary lookup through the system resolver fails on a boxd box. Most things still work only because HTTP(S) goes through the proxy at `127.0.0.1:17008`, and the pool resolves those names on its side. What breaks is exactly what ADR 0148 fixed for containers: anything that looks a name up before connecting (SSRF checks, `ssh`, `ping`, `dig`, raw sockets), plus anything that ignores the proxy settings. Nested Docker is fine, because it points its containers at `169.254.53.53` directly (26-10-15-760).

**Why nobody points it at the stub**

ADR 0148 §2 is about containers only: the pool *creates the container* with `--dns 169.254.53.53` (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/runtime.go:912`). A machine has no create-time DNS setting, and nothing on the machine path rewrites `/etc/resolv.conf`. The only code in the repo that touches that file is libkrun's.

There's also a catch that explains why boxd's resolver may have been left in place. Per 26-10-29-481 §2, the box reaches its pool by dialing the boxd host from `bridge.json`, here `dvm-prov-…--pool-dfqcve6ztdsmgbd6.boxd`, and it looks that name up through the provider on every dial. Only `10.40.0.1` can answer `*.boxd`. If you simply pointed `resolv.conf` at the stub, the stub would need the pool to answer, and reaching the pool needs a lookup that only boxd can answer.

**Fix I'd propose**
- On a machine, point `/etc/resolv.conf` at `169.254.53.53`, as a container effectively is.
- Have the bridge look up the pool's provider host with the provider's resolver directly, not through the system resolver. It would record the box's original nameserver before the rewrite.

That keeps the provider resolver for the one name only it can answer, and sends everything else through the pool, logged in the DNS audit trail like a container's.

# Machine-box findings: install paths, declared volumes, DNS

Found on boxd sandbox `sbx_yhg7pcs4by9bmsq5` (pool `dvm-pool-dfqcve6ztdsmgbd6`)
on 2026-11-02, where `discobox-harness-run` could not find `claude`, then
failed with `EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/var/lib/claude-code'`. Both were
worked around by hand in that box (`chmod o+x /home/boxd`, a `~/.local/bin/claude`
pin, a hand-made `/var/lib/claude-code`); none of that is a fix.

Read the package `DESIGN.md`/`REVIEW.md` files root-down before changing
anything, as `CLAUDE.md` says. Work items are in order of priority.

## 1. Bundles install into whatever directory the box's tools point at

### Root cause

boxd's base image installs Node with nvm under `/home/boxd/.nvm/...` and links
`/usr/local/bin/{node,npm,npx,corepack,claude,codex}` into `/home/boxd`, which is
`drwxr-x--- boxd:boxd`. The sandbox user (here uid 1002) cannot traverse it.

The node feature's adopt check (`sandbox-agent/provision/adopt.go`) is right:
it refuses that `node` because it resolves into a user's home, so the feature
*installs* Node (NodeSource, into `/usr/bin`). But every later step and runtime
script calls `npm`/`node` by bare name, and `/usr/local/bin` is ahead of
`/usr/bin` on every PATH, so they get the box's refused copy:

- `harness/claude-code/install-cli.sh` ran `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
  as root with boxd's npm, so Claude 2.1.316 went to
  `/home/boxd/.nvm/versions/node/v24.22.1/lib/node_modules/...`, invisible to the
  sandbox user. `/usr/local/bin/claude` stayed boxd's link to boxd's own 2.1.309.
- `discobox-agent-store status` said `image:` empty, because `image_version`
  only looks in `/usr/lib/node_modules` and `/usr/local/lib/node_modules`. So
  `pin` refused to pin the store's 2.1.316 (`cmd_pin` keeps the image's copy
  when it cannot read its version), and nothing on PATH was runnable.

A Node that fails only the *version floor* (say a reachable `/usr/local/bin/node`
v18) has the same effect: ours is installed and the old one keeps winning on
PATH, at provision time and at runtime.

### The rule to implement

Decided with the user:

- **Which Node runs is unchanged.** Adopt the box's Node/npm when it passes the
  adopt check (system PATH, every user can run it, not in a home, version
  floor). Do not install Node when one is usable. Install ours only when it is
  not.
- **Where our packages go is always ours.** Nothing Discobox installs with npm
  goes to npm's default global prefix. Harness CLIs and pnpm are installed with
  `--prefix` into a Discobox-owned directory (for example
  `/usr/local/lib/discobox/npm`), using the npm the node feature chose, by
  absolute path, never by PATH lookup.
- **Ours wins on PATH.** Each command from that prefix is linked into
  `/usr/local/bin`. When the node feature *installs* Node, `node`, `npm`, `npx`
  and `corepack` are linked there too. An existing `/usr/local/bin` entry that
  is dangling, or resolves into a user's home, is replaced. A box's own regular
  file that failed adoption must not keep shadowing ours either: move it aside
  (and record that you did) rather than silently deleting it. Pick a policy and
  write it down in the provision `DESIGN.md`.
- **Record the choice once.** The node feature should record the `node`/`npm`
  it adopted or installed (an env file under `/usr/local/lib/discobox/`, or the
  feature's entry in `provision.json`, whichever fits the provision contract
  better), so steps, the agent store and launchers read it instead of probing
  PATH. ADR 26-10-16-423 §4 says runtime integrations read reported outcomes
  rather than probe; follow that.

### Where it applies

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `harness/{claude-code,codex-cli,copilot,omp,opencode,pi}/install-cli.sh` | `npm install -g` → the chosen npm, `--prefix` into the Discobox prefix, then link its bins into `/usr/local/bin` |
| `sandbox-agent/features/node/install-pnpm.sh` | same (pnpm is not installed for anyone on that box today) |
| `sandbox-agent/features/node/install-node.sh` | when installing, make ours win on PATH as above |
| `sandbox-agent/features/node/agent-store` | `image_version` reads the Discobox prefix (`AGENT_IMAGE_DIRS` default); `fetch`/`refresh` use the recorded npm, not bare `npm` |
| `harness/*/capture.sh`, `harness/*/configure.sh`, `harness/codex-cli/launch.sh`, `harness/opencode/model.sh` | they run bare `node`; once `/usr/local/bin/node` is guaranteed to be the chosen Node this is fine, otherwise use the recorded path |
| `harness/*/check-launcher.sh` / provision checks | a step whose output landed in the wrong place must fail its check, so a box provisioned by the old scripts is repaired at its next boot |
| `sandbox-agent/provision/DESIGN.md`, `harness/DESIGN.md`, `sandbox-agent/REVIEW.md` | describe the rule; add a review rule: no bundle script runs a feature's tool by PATH lookup or installs into a tool's default global prefix |

The ADR's outcome table (26-10-16-423 §4) already says an installed feature goes
"into a prefix Discobox owns"; this brings the node feature in line, so no new
ADR is needed. Update `DESIGN.md`.

### Tests

- Unit-test the agent store's `image_version` against the new prefix.
- A provision test (or bats test, see `test/`) with a fake box: a
  `/usr/local/bin/node` that is a link into an unreadable `/home/x`, and one that
  is a reachable but too-old Node. Assert that the harness CLI lands in the
  Discobox prefix, `/usr/local/bin/<cli>` resolves to it, and the sandbox user
  can run it.

## 2. rustup is installed into root's home

`sandbox-agent/features/rust/install-rustup.sh` runs rustup's installer as root
with no `CARGO_HOME`, so rustup lands in `/root/.cargo`. The sandbox user has
no `rustup` or `cargo` (seen on this box). This does not depend on boxd, so it
likely affects every box; verify on a Docker sandbox too.

Fix: install rustup with `CARGO_HOME` set to a Discobox-owned directory (for
example `/usr/local/lib/discobox/rust`) and `--no-modify-path`, link the
proxies (`rustup`, `cargo`, `rustc`, `rustfmt`, `clippy-driver`, `cargo-*`)
into `/usr/local/bin`, and leave `RUSTUP_HOME` at its per-user default
`~/.rustup` (a declared cache volume) so toolchains stay per user. Users keep
their own `~/.cargo` for the registry and `cargo install` (also declared
volumes). The `rustup --version` guard must test the absolute path, not PATH.

## 3. Lower confidence: `uv` installs through a possible link

`sandbox-agent/features/python/install-uv.sh` installs with
`UV_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin`. If a box had `/usr/local/bin/uv` as a link into
a home, the installer might write through it. Not seen on boxd. Check what the
installer does with an existing link; if it follows it, apply item 1's
"replace a link into a home" rule first.

Checked and fine: `go` (its own `/usr/local/go`, earlier on PATH), `bun`
(`/usr/local`), `brew`, the apt tools (`mise`, `gh`, `direnv`), and
`shells-editors`, whose pattern (download into `/usr/local/lib/discobox/<tool>`,
link into `/usr/local/bin`) is the one to copy.

## 4. Declared volumes on a machine box: ADR 26-11-02-023

The `EACCES` on `/var/lib/claude-code`: Claude Code's harness declares that
path a `data` volume owned by the sandbox user and sets
`CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` to it. In a container `discobox-wire.service` creates and
mounts it from `/.discobox/data`; on a machine `boot.Provision` wires no
volumes (ADR 0126 §2), so nothing creates it.

The user wants machines wired exactly like containers. That is
`docs/adr/26-11-02-023-a-machine-sandbox-wires-its-declared-volumes-from-its-own-data-and-cache-roots.md`,
status **Proposed**. Per `CLAUDE.md`, land the ADR on its own (with its row in
`docs/adr/README.md`) and have the user accept it before implementing it. Then
implement it as written:

- `/.discobox/data` and `/.discobox/cache` on the machine's disk, wired with
  the same `volumeDir` layout, bind vs overlay rules and ownership.
- `discobox-wire.service` (`pkg/agentlayer/units/`) runs on machines too:
  conditioned on the placed `/etc/discobox/sandbox.json` there, before
  `sysinit.target`, on every boot; power off on failure on a machine, exit in
  a container.
- `pool-agent/sandboxruntime/machine.go` `place`: the first placement places
  without starting the agent or provisioning, then restarts the machine.
- `sandbox-agent/boot`: `Provision` stops skipping volumes; split what is
  per-boot wiring from what `provisionOnce` keeps.
- Update `sandbox-agent/DESIGN.md`, `pool-agent/DESIGN.md`, the unit's
  comment, the sandbox `discobox` skill's persistence table and the
  verify-recipes skill.

## 5. Not part of this task unless the user says so: machine DNS

On a machine box the DNS stub runs (`169.254.53.53:53`, and
`dig @169.254.53.53 github.com` answers), but `/etc/resolv.conf` still names the
provider's resolver (`10.40.0.1` on boxd), which answers `REFUSED` for anything
but `*.boxd`. So `getent hosts github.com` fails, and anything that resolves
before dialing (SSRF checks, `ssh`, `ping`) breaks; HTTP(S) works only because
the proxy resolves on the pool. ADR 0148 §2 sets `--dns 169.254.53.53` on
containers only (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/runtime.go:912`), and nothing does
the machine's equivalent.

The catch: the bridge reaches the pool by dialing the provider host in
`bridge.json` (`address`, here `…--pool-….boxd`), resolved through the
provider at every dial (ADR 26-10-29-481 §2). Pointing `resolv.conf` at the
stub alone would make reaching the pool depend on the pool. Proposed fix: on a
machine, point `resolv.conf` at the stub, and have the bridge resolve the
pool's provider host against the box's original nameserver, recorded before
the rewrite, directly rather than through libc. That extends 0148 §2, so it
needs an ADR; the user has not decided yet whether it is its own or part of
26-11-02-023.

## Finishing

Run `go tool task check-hooks` before handing back, and `go tool task ci:check`
for the Dockerfile and shellcheck parts. Commit to the branch that is checked
out; do not create branches.
